paras: The attempted lynching of Alfred Ross took place in Memphis, Tennessee, on the evening of July 24, 1882, when a crowd tried to hang Ross, a Black steamboat roustabout, as officers brought him out to be identified. Ross had been accused that morning of striking an aged Italian grocer, John Genochio, with a rock. Bystanders held the crowd back, and Ross was later bound over to the Criminal Court.

Genochio, said to be over seventy, kept a small grocery on the Poplar street boulevard opposite the residence of Col. H. A. Montgomery. According to the Memphis Appeal, he had been assaulted and robbed once before, and the Public Ledger called the July attack the third attempt in a few years to kill and rob him.

The Appeal reported that about 10 o'clock a man came into the store, bought sugar and coffee, and struck Genochio on the head with a large rock as he bent to get nails; the Ledger put the time at about 11. A body of men pursued the fleeing suspect on foot and on horseback for over a mile, and he surrendered at the sight of a pistol with nearly all his clothes torn off. He was identified as Alfred Ross, a roustabout on the steamer Halliday, and placed in the station-house.

That evening, the Ledger reported, officers took Ross out to be identified, and "a crowd of exasperated people" gathered and "showed a disposition to lynch" him. In the paper's words he "made a narrow miss from being swung to a limb," but the crowd was restrained by several persons in the vicinity. The place of the identification is not named, and no number is given for the crowd.

Ross denied the assault, saying he had gone to the country after a quarrel with his wife and ran because men came at him with pistols; questioned by Chief Davis, his wife denied any quarrel and said he had stayed with her Sunday night. His police court hearing was put off until Thursday, with his defense given as an alibi. On July 27 Genochio, his head bandaged, and four others identified Ross, including Genochio's employee Charles Boyd and Smart Mootry, a boy working for Montgomery; the defense offered no testimony, and President Hadden bound Ross over to the Criminal Court.

A grand jury was to take up the case within days, and the Criminal Court calendar set case No. 18, Alfred Ross, for September 21, 1882. No report of an indictment, a verdict or a sentence appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowd is reported to have been arrested.

Only the two Memphis dailies covered the case, and only the Public Ledger mentioned the lynching threat, in a short item that called Ross "the murderous scoundrel" and the would-be lynchers "exasperated." The Ledger had headlined its first report "Desperate Darky's Deed," and later described Ross as looking "like a dare devil criminal." The Appeal opened its long account by calling the attack "committed as usual by a negro ruffian" and warned that it would "go hard with the negro" if Genochio died, yet it also printed Ross's denial and his wife's statement. No paper outside Memphis was found carrying the story.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Alfred Ross
bases: A crowd gathered and 'showed a disposition to lynch' Ross, a Black prisoner, while officers had him out for identification, but was restrained and no one was killed (A2).
A crowd threatened to hang Ross over the assault on Genochio but was held back, and he survived to be bound over to the Criminal Court (A2, A7); this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Only the Public Ledger reports the lynching threat (A2); the Appeal's detailed account of the same day mentions the pursuit and capture but no crowd at the identification (A5).

accounts.label: Public Ledger
accounts.gist: Ross was nearly hanged when officers took him out to be identified; an exasperated crowd was restrained by several persons nearby.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: Describes the assault, a pursuit of over a mile on foot and horseback, and Ross's surrender at pistol point with his clothes nearly torn off; does not mention a lynching threat.

accounts.label: Ross's own account
accounts.gist: Ross denied the assault, said he had gone to the country after a fuss with his wife and ran because men came at him with pistols; his defense was an alibi.

framing.detail: The Ledger headlined the assault 'Desperate Darky's Deed', called Ross 'the murderous scoundrel' and the would-be lynchers 'a crowd of exasperated people', without criticizing them.
The Appeal called the assault 'committed as usual by a negro ruffian' and warned 'It will go hard with the negro' if Genochio died, while printing Ross's denial and his wife's statement.
